title: Shared national pride coexists with unequal community safety and a gap between cultural recognition and political trust
source_unit: My Code, Culture 360 Political Tracker Wave 15: Beyond the Vote: Why Midterm Persuasion Requires Cultural Relevance
geography: United States; eligible voters ages 18–64, with Hispanic, Black, AANHPI, and non-multicultural comparison groups

observations.period: July 2026 Wave 15; national pride and perceived political-violence risk

denominator.unit: U.S. eligible voters ages 18–64 in the My Code Wave 15 online survey

national_pride.value: roughly three-quarters in every community say they are proud to be American

political_violence_concern.unit: percent of eligible voters concerned about political violence

community_risk_difference.unit: percent among respondents concerned about political violence who say their own community faces greater risk than others

pride_safety_gap.value: shared national identity does not imply shared experience of safety

observations.method: Weighted online survey fielded through July 8, 2026; reported unweighted bases are Hispanic n=651, Black n=650, AANHPI n=628, and non-multicultural n=1,243. Risk figures are based on 2,781 respondents concerned about political violence.
observations.uncertainty: The study measures perceptions and self-identification, not verified exposure to violence, objective community risk, or causal effects of campaign messages.
observations.subgroup: Hispanic, Black, AANHPI, and non-multicultural eligible voters ages 18–64.
observations.counterinterpretation: Differences may reflect local context, news exposure, partisanship, socioeconomic conditions, or question interpretation rather than an intrinsic group-level safety condition.

observations.period: July 2026 Wave 15; cultural recognition and political trust

denominator.unit: U.S. eligible voters ages 18–64 in the My Code Wave 15 online survey; subgroup bases vary

black_understood_consideration.unit: percent of Black eligible voters saying feeling understood would increase candidate consideration

black_understood_trust.unit: percent of Black eligible voters saying feeling understood would increase trust

non_multicultural_consideration.unit: percent of non-multicultural voters saying feeling understood would increase consideration

non_multicultural_trust.unit: percent of non-multicultural voters saying feeling understood would increase trust

recognition_trust_gap.value: being understood can open consideration without transferring into trust

observations.method: Weighted cross-sectional survey estimates on the stated effects of feeling understood; the release does not publish the full question wording or all subgroup confidence intervals.
observations.uncertainty: Consideration and trust are stated attitudinal responses, not observed vote choice, candidate evaluation, message exposure, or durable institutional legitimacy.
observations.subgroup: Black and non-multicultural eligible voters, with the wider tracker also reporting Hispanic and AANHPI groups.
observations.counterinterpretation: The difference may reflect baseline trust, candidate context, political identity, wording, or different meanings attached to being understood rather than a universal conversion rule.

observations.period: July 2026 Wave 15; prior vote continuity and participation uncertainty

denominator.unit: U.S. eligible voters ages 18–64 in the My Code Wave 15 online survey

repeat_2024_choice.unit: percent saying they would repeat their 2024 vote choice

nonparticipation.unit: percent saying they would not vote

uncertainty.unit: percent unsure what they would do

vote_switching.unit: percent saying they would vote differently

persuadability_boundary.value: reduced vote continuity is not equivalent to candidate openness because nonparticipation and uncertainty are separate routes

observations.method: Wave 15 comparison with Wave 14 from the Culture 360 Political Tracker; the release reports the percentage-point change and response categories.
observations.uncertainty: These are hypothetical or stated intentions during an election cycle, not validated turnout, eventual vote choice, or causal response to campaign communication.
observations.subgroup: Multicultural eligible voters and the broader eligible-voter sample ages 18–64; detailed group bases are not supplied for every response category in the release.
observations.counterinterpretation: A lower repeat-choice share can reflect dissatisfaction, uncertainty, abstention, measurement timing, or changing candidate fields rather than persuasion opportunity.

observations.period: July 2026 Wave 15; issue pressure and information overload

denominator.unit: U.S. eligible voters ages 18–64 in the My Code Wave 15 online survey

cost_of_goods.unit: percent naming cost of goods as a leading household concern overall

aanhpi_cost_of_goods.unit: percent of AANHPI voters naming cost of goods as a leading concern

black_hispanic_housing.unit: percent of Black and Hispanic voters naming housing as a leading concern

political_news_overload.value: between 52% and 67% across communities feel overwhelmed by the daily volume of political news

issue_to_attention_route.value: material concerns and political-news overload may constrain how cultural messages become usable political attention

observations.method: Weighted cross-sectional online survey with community-specific reporting of household concerns and political-news volume.
observations.uncertainty: Concern and overwhelm are self-reported; the release does not establish whether information volume causes nonparticipation, issue prioritization, or message rejection.
observations.subgroup: Hispanic, Black, AANHPI, non-multicultural, and overall eligible-voter groups.
observations.counterinterpretation: News overload can coexist with high engagement and may reflect political salience rather than disengagement; issue shares are not household expenditure or housing-cost measures.

related_sources.claim: My Code release reports Wave 15 field dates, sample, subgroup bases, and topline cultural-political findings.
Gallup/Kettering provides a separate broad democratic-performance and local-national legitimacy comparison.

boundary: This record adds a sponsor-produced cultural-political mechanism: national pride can coexist with unequal community safety perceptions; cultural recognition can increase consideration without producing trust; and weakening vote continuity can split into switching, uncertainty, and nonparticipation. It does not establish objective community risk, causal persuasion, validated turnout, or durable trust change.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official My Code release carried by PR Newswire was reviewed for Wave 15 field dates, overall and subgroup bases, pride/safety, recognition/trust, vote-continuity, household-concern, and political-news-overload findings.
